content.prompt: Trapezia $BCFE$ and $EFDA$ are similar. Find the value of $y$.

answer.worked:
Corresponding bases are $BC\leftrightarrow EF$ and $EF\leftrightarrow AD$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{y}{6}&=\frac{6}{4}\\y&=\frac{6}{4}\times6\\y&=9\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: The student must read the stated similarity BCFE ~ EFDA and see that EF is the long base of the upper trapezium and the short base of the lower one. They then pair BC with EF and EF with AD, set up y/6 = 6/4 and solve. This is a single linear proportion with a one-step solve. The unknown is the larger base, so there is no quadratic or square root, which makes it easier than the same configuration with the middle base unknown (p34-q5). It is harder than the plain triangle correspondences in p32-q2 because one segment plays two roles and no side pairing is shown. It is a routine linked procedure, with no unsignposted insight, and sits just below A4.

content.prompt: Determine the value of $x$.

answer.worked:
Match the sides using the vertex symbols.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x}{4}&=\frac{9}{x}\\x^2&=4\times9\\x^2&=36\\x&=6\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
Take the positive value because $x$ is a length.

answer.worked:

children.label: a
children.prompt: A street lamp is $8\text{ m}$ high. A boy stands $7\text{ m}$ from the base of the lamp and his shadow is $3\text{ m}$ long. Find the height of the boy.

answer.worked:
The large triangle's ground length is $3+7=10\text{ m}$.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{10}{3}h&=8\\h&=8\times\frac{3}{10}\\h&=2.4\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: A boy is $1.5\text{ m}$ tall. He stands $6\text{ m}$ from the base of a street lamp and his shadow is $2\text{ m}$ long. Find the height of the lamp.

answer.worked:
The large triangle's ground length is $2+6=8\text{ m}$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Scale factor}&=\frac{8}{2}=4\\H&=1.5\times4\\H&=6\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A street lamp is $5$ m high. When a girl stands $6$ m from the base of the lamp her shadow is $1.8$ m long. Calculate the height of the girl, to the nearest centimetre.

spec.description: Editable schematic with the shadow tip, girl and lamp in left-to-right order. Adjacent ground intervals are 1.8 m and 6 m; one straight light ray passes through the girl's top and the lamp's top.
spec.mathematics: The larger triangle has horizontal length 6+1.8=7.8 m and vertical height 5 m. The smaller triangle has horizontal length 1.8 m and unknown girl height.

answer.worked:
The lamp-to-shadow-tip distance is $6+1.8=7.8$ m. Let the girl's height be $h$ metres. The triangles are similar.
$$\begin{aligned}\frac{h}{5}&=\frac{1.8}{7.8}\\h&=5\times\frac{1.8}{7.8}\\h&=\frac{15}{13}\text{ m}\\h&=\frac{1500}{13}\text{ cm}\\h&\approx115\text{ cm}\end{aligned}$$
The girl is $115$ cm tall, to the nearest centimetre.

The distance is $1.4\text{ km}$.

content.prompt:
A standard volleyball net is $2.73$ metres tall.
Martin stands $1$ metre away from the net.
He jumps and spikes a volleyball directly to the ground on the opposite side of the net.
If his hand is $3.35$ metres above the ground when he spikes and the ball passes just above the net, find the distance between the volleyball and the net as it lands on the other side.
Write your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

answer.short:
$4.4\text{ m}$

The two right triangles are similar, so $\frac{2.73}{3.35}=\frac{x}{x+1}$.
answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the distance from the net to where the ball lands.
The two right triangles are similar, so:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{2.73}{3.35}&=\frac{x}{x+1}\\2.73(x+1)&=3.35x\\2.73x+2.73&=3.35x\\2.73&=0.62x\\x&=4.403\ldots\end{align*}$$
The distance is $4.4\text{ m}$.

inlines.text: A map maker wants to make a map of an area that is
She decides to use a scale of
. Explain why this map scale is not appropriate.

answer.short: The map would be $80\text{ m}\times80\text{ m}$, which is impractically large.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Actual side length}&=8\text{ km}=8000\text{ m}\\\text{Map side length}&=8000\text{ m}\div100\\&=80\text{ m}\end{align*}$$
Both sides have the same length, so the map would be $80\text{ m}\times80\text{ m}$. This is too large for a practical map.

inlines.text: A scientist shows a photomicrograph image of a 10 cm long cell.

answer.short: The ratio is reversed. Magnification should be $100\,000:1$, since the image is larger than the actual cell.
answer.worked: Scales are written in image : original order. A scale of $1:100\,000$ means the image is smaller than the original, so it represents a reduction. For magnification by $100\,000$, the ratio should be $100\,000:1$.

Worked example: A street lamp is $6\text{ m}$ high. A girl stands $4.5\text{ m}$ from the base of the lamp and her shadow is $1.5\text{ m}$ long. Find the height of the girl.
The girl and the lamp make two similar triangles. The large triangle's ground length is the shadow plus the distance from the lamp.
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} & \text{Small} & \text{Large}\\\hline \text{Height} & h & 6\\ \text{Ground} & 1.5 & 1.5+4.5=6\end{array}$$
$$\begin{align*}\text{Scale factor}&=\frac{6}{1.5}=4\\4h&=6\\\frac{4h}{\color{#ef6068}{4}}&=\frac{6}{\color{#ef6068}{4}}\\h&=1.5\text{ m}\end{align*}$$
The girl is $1.5\text{ m}$ tall.

[Pedagogy audit v2 · Applied automatically · Definition] The current definition would count any freehand sketch as a scale drawing. Replace the first sentence so every length is a fixed multiple of the matching real-life length, and add that a scale of n:1 means the drawing is larger than the original.
Replacement text: A **scale drawing** is a drawing of a real-life object in which every length is the same fixed multiple of the matching real-life length. The drawing can be smaller or larger than the object.

Examples include maps, house plans, and scientific diagrams.

We call the real-life object the **original**, and the drawing the **image**.

Scales for scale drawings are written in **simplified ratio notation:**

$$\begin{gathered}\text{image}:\text{original}\\ 1:n\end{gathered}$$

A scale of $1:500$ means every 1 unit on the drawing is 500 units in real life. A scale of $n:1$ means the drawing is larger than the original.

1. Set up a ratio table **_image : original_**
  a. The first row should be the given scale.
  b. The second row should be the given length and the length you want to find.
2. Find the unknown side by multiplying or dividing.

Scale Factor
• Similar figures have corresponding sides in the same ratio.
• This ratio is called the scale factor, k.
• The scale factor is the number you multiply the original shape by to get the image.
entries.presentation: Light blue activity band above information and a native three-column table.

entries.description:
Three columns, in order:
Reduction: k < 1; the image is smaller than the original.
Congruent: k = 1; the image is identical, or congruent, to the original.
Enlargement: k > 1; the image is larger than the original.
entries.presentation: Preserve column headings, relationships and meaningful table borders; no response cells.

Each has a right-angle marker at its lower-left vertex. A left-pointing arrow from the original towards the reduced triangle is labelled “Scale factor 0.5”. A right-pointing arrow from the original towards the enlarged triangle is labelled “Scale factor 2”.

entries.description: Finding Lengths in Scale Drawings

Scale Drawings
A scale drawing is a smaller or larger drawing of a real-life object.
Examples include maps, house plans, and scientific diagrams.
We call the real-life object the original, and the drawing the image.
Scales for scale drawings are written in simplified ratio notation:

image : original
1 : n
